content: Toxicodendron is a genus of woody plants, including trees, shrubs, and vines, belonging to the family Anacardiaceae, commonly known as the sumac family. All members of this genus produce urushiol, a skin-irritating oil that can cause severe allergic reactions. The genus name Toxicodendron translates to poison tree. While some taxonomists have historically included these plants in the genus Rhus, molecular evidence supports maintaining Toxicodendron as a distinct monophyletic genus. The plants in this genus typically have alternately arranged, pinnately compound leaves and bear whitish or grayish drupes. In North America, the most well-known species are poison ivy, which is widespread in eastern regions, and poison oak, which is common in the western parts of the continent. These plants exhibit significant variability in appearance. Their leaves may have smooth, toothed, or lobed edges, and all three types of leaf margins can sometimes be found on a single plant. Toxicodendron species can grow as creeping vines, climbing vines, shrubs, or, in the case of species like the lacquer tree and poison sumac, as trees. Poison ivy and poison oak typically have leaves with three leaflets, though some plants may have five or even seven. Poison sumac leaves usually have 7–13 leaflets, while the lacquer tree has 7–19 leaflets. The common names of these plants are derived from their resemblance to unrelated species and the allergic reactions caused by urushiol. For example, poison oak is not a true oak (genus Quercus, family Fagaceae) but is named for its superficial similarity to white oak leaves. Similarly, poison ivy is not a true ivy (genus Hedera, family Araliaceae) but has a similar growth habit. Both poison oak and poison ivy belong to the sumac family, Anacardiaceae. It is important to note that these plants do not contain a true poison but rather a potent allergen. The resins of certain Asian species, such as Toxicodendron vernicifluum (lacquer tree) and Toxicodendron succedaneum (wax tree), are used to produce lacquer. As a byproduct of lacquer production, the berries of these species are used to make Japan wax. Avoidance, Treatment, and Safety For detailed information on preventing and treating rashes caused by Toxicodendron species, refer to resources on urushiol-induced contact dermatitis. Species of Toxicodendron 1. Western Poison Oak (Toxicodendron diversilobum or Rhus diversiloba) Found throughout much of western North America, from the Pacific coast to the Sierra Nevada and Cascade mountain ranges, extending from southern British Columbia to Baja California. It is extremely common in this region and is California's most prevalent woody shrub. Western poison oak is highly variable in appearance, growing as a dense shrub in sunny areas or as a climbing vine in shaded regions. It reproduces via creeping rootstocks or seeds. The leaves are divided into three leaflets, 35–100 mm long, with scalloped, toothed, or lobed edges. Californians often recognize it by the rhyme, leaves of three, let it be. The leaves can appear red, yellow, green, or a combination of these colors, depending on the season. 2. Asian Poison Ivy (Toxicodendron orientale or Rhus orientale) This species closely resembles American poison ivy and replaces it throughout East Asia. Some texts treat it as a variety of the American species. 3. Potanin's Lacquer Tree or Chinese Varnish Tree (Toxicodendron potaninii or Rhus potaninii) Native to central China, this species is similar to Toxicodendron vernicifluum but typically has fewer leaflets per leaf. It can grow up to 20 meters tall and is used for lacquer production. Its leaves usually have 7–9 leaflets. 4. Poison Ivy (Toxicodendron radicans or Rhus radicans) Extremely common in parts of North America, poison ivy grows in all U.S. states except Alaska, Hawaii, and California. It is less common in western North America but also grows in Central America. Poison ivy can appear as a creeping vine, climbing vine, or shrub and reproduces via creeping rootstocks and seeds. Its leaves, arranged alternately, are usually in groups of three and measure 20–50 mm in length. The leaves may be pointed, toothed, smooth, or lobed but are never serrated. They can be shiny or dull, with color varying by season. The vines grow almost straight upward rather than wrapping around their support and can reach heights of 8–10 meters. In some cases, poison ivy vines may engulf their supporting structure, giving the appearance of a poison ivy tree. 5. Western Poison Ivy (Toxicodendron rydbergii or Rhus rydbergii) Found in northern parts of the eastern United States, as well as in western U.S. and Canada, this species is less common than poison oak in the west. It may grow as a vine or shrub and was once considered a subspecies of poison ivy. It sometimes hybridizes with climbing species. Western poison ivy is found in much of western and central North America but is rare in the eastern U.S. south of New England. 6. Wax Tree (Toxicodendron succedaneum or Rhus succedanea) Native to Asia, this species has been planted in other regions, including Australia and New Zealand, where it is now classified as a noxious weed. It is a large shrub or tree, up to 8 meters tall, resembling a sumac tree. Due to its attractive autumn foliage, it has been planted as an ornamental plant, often by gardeners unaware of its allergenic properties. The fatty-acid methyl ester of its kernel oil meets major biodiesel standards in the U.S., Germany, and the European Union. 7. Atlantic Poison Oak (Toxicodendron pubescens or Rhus toxicarium) Found mostly in sandy soils in the eastern United States, this shrub has leaves in groups of three. The leaves are typically rounded or lobed and densely haired. Although often confused with poison ivy, Atlantic poison oak can be distinguished by the small clumps of hair on the veins on the underside of its leaves, which poison ivy lacks. 8. Lacquer Tree or Varnish Tree (Toxicodendron vernicifluum or Rhus verniciflua) Native to Asia, particularly China and Japan, this tree can grow up to 20 meters tall. Its sap produces a highly durable lacquer. The leaves have 7–19 leaflets, most often 11–13. The sap contains urushiol, the allergenic oil responsible for contact dermatitis. The name urushiol is derived from the Japanese name for this species, urushi. Other names for this species include Japanese lacquer tree, Japanese varnish tree, and Japanese sumac. 9. Poison Sumac (Toxicodendron vernix or Rhus vernix) This tall shrub or small tree, ranging from 2–7 meters in height, grows in swampy, open areas and reproduces by seeds. Its leaves have 7–13 untoothed leaflets arranged in a feather-compound pattern. Poison sumac is significantly more virulent in causing urushiol-induced contact dermatitis than other Toxicodendron species, including poison ivy and poison oak. Some botanists consider poison sumac the most toxic plant species in the United States.
